parts.name: Passage 1
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1.

Reef Fish Study

Tom Holmes examines the relationship between size and survival in fish on Australia's Great Barrier Reef

It is widely believed among those who study animals that larger size confers some form of advantage throughout life. The possibility that certain body characteristics may influence an animal’s chances of surviving a predatory attack has received considerable attention and has been investigated across a wide range of species and habitats. Body size, weight, growth rate, overall condition, sensory development and escape speed have all been linked to survival. Of these, body size has received the most attention from researchers, leading to the development of several theories about how it may influence the predator–prey relationship. One of the most popular is known as the ‘bigger is better’ hypothesis. This theory predicts that greater body size should improve an individual’s ability to escape from predators because it is associated with characteristics such as strength and visual development. Bigger is generally thought to be better, but this is not necessarily the case for every species or at every stage of life.

Compared with other habitats and ecosystems, relatively little is known about predator–prey relationships within tropical reef communities. What is known is largely limited to predator identity and, to some extent, what these predators eat. Much less is understood about what drives these interactions or how body size influences their outcome. These questions have led our research team to Lizard Island, in the northern sector of the Great Barrier Reef. We want to examine predator–prey interactions around settlement, when tropical fish move from the larval phase into the early juvenile stage. We also want to determine whether predators choose prey according to characteristics such as the prey’s size, weight and swimming speed, all of which vary among individuals at the beginning of the juvenile stage.

Most coral reef fish have a life cycle consisting of an open-ocean larval phase followed by juvenile and adult stages near the reef. The transition from the larval to the juvenile stage involves rapid and dramatic physical changes and a sudden move from the open ocean to coral reef habitats. This transition is commonly known as ‘settlement’. Mortality is particularly high during the first 48 hours after settlement, as individuals must adapt both to life on the reef and to a previously unknown set of predators.

However, studying predator–prey interactions around settlement is no easy task. On the northern Great Barrier Reef, coral reef fish settlement usually occurs within 2–3 days of a new moon during the warmer summer months. These short windows of opportunity, combined with the difficulties of working underwater, transporting fish and acclimatising them to laboratory conditions, often make research a daunting task. These obstacles are overcome through a combination of innovative techniques, long working hours and sheer persistence. Immediately before settlement, we collect larval fish using purpose-built traps that use artificial light to attract and retain only fish at this life stage. The larval fish, together with predatory fish, are then transported to an aquarium before being used in a series of aquarium-based and field-based trials.

According to the ‘bigger is better’ hypothesis, individuals that are larger at settlement should have a greater chance of surviving predator attacks immediately afterwards. However, our initial research suggests that this is not always true. There may be several reasons for this.

Reef predator communities can differ considerably over relatively short distances. Species that are abundant in one location may be particularly rare in a similar habitat just 100 metres away. Just as predators differ in the types of prey they favour, they also differ in the sizes of prey they prefer. These preferences are influenced by predators’ physical characteristics, such as mouth size, as well as by behavioural differences between species. As a result, the predator community into which a reef fish settles may determine which individuals survive.

A further explanation for why larger individuals do not survive more often than smaller fish during this period may lie in an alternative hypothesis known as ‘optimal foraging theory’. According to this theory, being either very large or very small may reduce the likelihood of being selected as prey. Predators are expected to favour individuals that provide the greatest energy return. This generally involves a trade-off between the energy gained from eating a fish and the amount of energy required to catch it. Larger prey provide a higher energy return, but smaller prey generally require less energy to catch. This usually results in a preference for medium-sized prey.

At the time of settlement, juvenile reef fish vary in the characteristics that can help them survive a predatory attack. However, these characteristics are not strongly associated with body size. For example, larger individuals are not necessarily faster, which means that they may be no harder to catch than smaller prey. If this is the case, the usual trade-off is altered and, according to optimal foraging theory, predators should prefer larger prey because of their greater energy return. Consequently, larger individuals may be targeted by some predators at the time of settlement. Our research aims to determine whether larger size may, in fact, be a distinct disadvantage during certain life stages.

parts.name: Passage 2
parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

Are Artists Liars?

A.

Shortly before his death, Marlon Brando was working on a series of instructional videos about acting, to be called “Lying for a Living”. In the surviving footage, Brando can be seen dispensing gnomic advice on his craft to a group of enthusiastic, if somewhat bemused, Hollywood stars, including Leonardo DiCaprio and Sean Penn. Brando also recruited people at random from the streets of Los Angeles and persuaded them to improvise; the footage is said to include a memorable scene featuring two dwarves and a giant Samoan. “If you can lie, you can act,” Brando told Jod Kaftan, a writer for Rolling Stone and one of the few people to have viewed the footage. “Are you good at lying?” asked Kaftan. “Jesus,” said Brando, “I’m fabulous at it.”

B.

Brando was not the first person to note that the line between an artist and a liar is a fine one. If art is a kind of lying, then lying is a form of art, albeit of a lower order—as Oscar Wilde and Mark Twain have observed. Indeed, lying and artistic storytelling spring from a common neurological root—one revealed in the cases of psychiatric patients who suffer from a particular kind of impairment. Both liars and artists refuse to accept the tyranny of reality. Both carefully craft convincing stories—a skill requiring intellectual sophistication, emotional sensitivity and physical self-control. In this sense, liars are both writers and performers of their own work. Such parallels are hardly coincidental.

C.

A case study published in 1985 by neurologist Antonio Damasio describes a middle-aged woman whose brain had been damaged by a series of strokes. Although she retained abilities such as coherent speech, what she said was often unpredictable. In psychiatric terms, she was “confabulating”. Chronic confabulation is a rare memory disorder defined as the production of fabricated, distorted or misinterpreted memories without a conscious intention to deceive. Whereas amnesiacs make errors of omission—leaving gaps they cannot fill—confabulators make errors of commission: they invent information. They are also usually unaware of their condition and may sincerely offer highly implausible explanations of their circumstances. One patient, for example, claimed that a teenage girl had shot him three times in the head during the Second World War, killing him, before surgery brought him back to life. Confabulators are not trying to deceive anyone. They engage in what neuropsychologist Morris Moscovitch calls “honest lying”. Faced with uncertainty, they may experience a “compulsion to narrate”: a deep-seated need to shape, order and explain what they do not understand. They can also be highly inventive with language; one patient, asked what happened to Queen Marie Antoinette, replied that she had been “suicided” by her family. In this respect, confabulators can resemble novelists in their ability to turn almost anything into material. Unlike writers, however, they have little or no control over what they produce.

D.

The wider significance of this condition lies in what it tells us about ourselves. Evidently, there is a gushing river of verbal creativity in the normal human mind, from which both artistic invention and lying are drawn. We are born storytellers, spinning narrative out of our experience and imagination and straining against the leash that keeps us tethered to reality. This is a wonderful thing; it gives us the ability to conceive of alternative futures and different worlds. It also helps us to understand our own lives through the entertaining stories of others. But it can lead us into trouble, particularly when we try to persuade others that our inventions are real. Most of the time, as our stories bubble up to consciousness, we exercise our cerebral censors, controlling which stories we tell and to whom. Yet people lie for all sorts of reasons, including the fact that making things up can be dangerously fun.

E.

During a high-profile libel case in 1996, Jonathan Aitken, a former cabinet minister, challenged claims made by the Guardian about his relationships with Saudi arms dealers, including meetings he allegedly held with them during a trip to Paris. During the case, Aitken also recounted a story to illustrate the difficulties he had endured after the newspaper damaged his reputation. He claimed that after journalists confronted him outside his home, he drove away with his daughter and was pursued through central London by reporters in a van. What amazed many in hindsight was the sheer superfluity of the lies Aitken told during his testimony. Some were needed to sustain his original story, but others seemed to be told simply for the pleasure of invention. His charm, fluency and flair for theatrical displays of sincerity made it appear that he might win the case. However, a documentary crew later produced unedited footage showing that Aitken’s daughter had not been with him that day and that he had simply driven away, with no vehicle in pursuit. The case finally collapsed in June 1997, when the defence found indisputable evidence concerning his Paris trip.

F.

Of course, unlike Aitken, actors, playwrights and novelists are not literally attempting to deceive us, because the convention is understood in advance: audiences enter a theatre or open a novel knowing that what follows is invented. Perhaps this is why art was invented in the first place—as a safe space into which our lies can be corralled and channelled into something socially useful. Given the universal compulsion to tell stories, art is the best way to refine and enjoy the particularly outlandish or insightful ones. But that is not the whole story. The key way in which artistic “lies” differ from ordinary lies and from the “honest lying” of chronic confabulators is that they carry meaning and resonance beyond their creator. Liars lie on their own behalf; artists tell lies on behalf of everyone. If writers share a compulsion to narrate, they direct it towards finding insights into the human condition. Mario Vargas Llosa has written that novels “express a curious truth that can only be expressed in a furtive and veiled fashion, masquerading as what it is not.” Art is a lie whose secret ingredient is truth.

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2.

Are Artists Liars?

A.

Shortly before his death, Marlon Brando was working on a series of instructional videos about acting, to be called “Lying for a Living”. In the surviving footage, Brando can be seen dispensing gnomic advice on his craft to a group of enthusiastic, if somewhat bemused, Hollywood stars, including Leonardo DiCaprio and Sean Penn. Brando also recruited people at random from the streets of Los Angeles and persuaded them to improvise; the footage is said to include a memorable scene featuring two dwarves and a giant Samoan. “If you can lie, you can act,” Brando told Jod Kaftan, a writer for Rolling Stone and one of the few people to have viewed the footage. “Are you good at lying?” asked Kaftan. “Jesus,” said Brando, “I’m fabulous at it.”

B.

Brando was not the first person to note that the line between an artist and a liar is a fine one. If art is a kind of lying, then lying is a form of art, albeit of a lower order—as Oscar Wilde and Mark Twain have observed. Indeed, lying and artistic storytelling spring from a common neurological root—one revealed in the cases of psychiatric patients who suffer from a particular kind of impairment. Both liars and artists refuse to accept the tyranny of reality. Both carefully craft convincing stories—a skill requiring intellectual sophistication, emotional sensitivity and physical self-control. In this sense, liars are both writers and performers of their own work. Such parallels are hardly coincidental.

C.

A case study published in 1985 by neurologist Antonio Damasio describes a middle-aged woman whose brain had been damaged by a series of strokes. Although she retained abilities such as coherent speech, what she said was often unpredictable. In psychiatric terms, she was “confabulating”. Chronic confabulation is a rare memory disorder defined as the production of fabricated, distorted or misinterpreted memories without a conscious intention to deceive. Whereas amnesiacs make errors of omission—leaving gaps they cannot fill—confabulators make errors of commission: they invent information. They are also usually unaware of their condition and may sincerely offer highly implausible explanations of their circumstances. One patient, for example, claimed that a teenage girl had shot him three times in the head during the Second World War, killing him, before surgery brought him back to life. Confabulators are not trying to deceive anyone. They engage in what neuropsychologist Morris Moscovitch calls “honest lying”. Faced with uncertainty, they may experience a “compulsion to narrate”: a deep-seated need to shape, order and explain what they do not understand. They can also be highly inventive with language; one patient, asked what happened to Queen Marie Antoinette, replied that she had been “suicided” by her family. In this respect, confabulators can resemble novelists in their ability to turn almost anything into material. Unlike writers, however, they have little or no control over what they produce.

D.

The wider significance of this condition lies in what it tells us about ourselves. Evidently, there is a gushing river of verbal creativity in the normal human mind, from which both artistic invention and lying are drawn. We are born storytellers, spinning narrative out of our experience and imagination and straining against the leash that keeps us tethered to reality. This is a wonderful thing; it gives us the ability to conceive of alternative futures and different worlds. It also helps us to understand our own lives through the entertaining stories of others. But it can lead us into trouble, particularly when we try to persuade others that our inventions are real. Most of the time, as our stories bubble up to consciousness, we exercise our cerebral censors, controlling which stories we tell and to whom. Yet people lie for all sorts of reasons, including the fact that making things up can be dangerously fun.

E.

During a high-profile libel case in 1996, Jonathan Aitken, a former cabinet minister, challenged claims made by the Guardian about his relationships with Saudi arms dealers, including meetings he allegedly held with them during a trip to Paris. During the case, Aitken also recounted a story to illustrate the difficulties he had endured after the newspaper damaged his reputation. He claimed that after journalists confronted him outside his home, he drove away with his daughter and was pursued through central London by reporters in a van. What amazed many in hindsight was the sheer superfluity of the lies Aitken told during his testimony. Some were needed to sustain his original story, but others seemed to be told simply for the pleasure of invention. His charm, fluency and flair for theatrical displays of sincerity made it appear that he might win the case. However, a documentary crew later produced unedited footage showing that Aitken’s daughter had not been with him that day and that he had simply driven away, with no vehicle in pursuit. The case finally collapsed in June 1997, when the defence found indisputable evidence concerning his Paris trip.

F.

Of course, unlike Aitken, actors, playwrights and novelists are not literally attempting to deceive us, because the convention is understood in advance: audiences enter a theatre or open a novel knowing that what follows is invented. Perhaps this is why art was invented in the first place—as a safe space into which our lies can be corralled and channelled into something socially useful. Given the universal compulsion to tell stories, art is the best way to refine and enjoy the particularly outlandish or insightful ones. But that is not the whole story. The key way in which artistic “lies” differ from ordinary lies and from the “honest lying” of chronic confabulators is that they carry meaning and resonance beyond their creator. Liars lie on their own behalf; artists tell lies on behalf of everyone. If writers share a compulsion to narrate, they direct it towards finding insights into the human condition. Mario Vargas Llosa has written that novels “express a curious truth that can only be expressed in a furtive and veiled fashion, masquerading as what it is not.” Art is a lie whose secret ingredient is truth.

parts.passageHtml:
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3.

From ancient times to the present, historians have asked the same question: how and why did an ordinary little town in central Italy grow so much larger than any other in the ancient Mediterranean and come to control such a vast empire? During the first century BCE, Roman writers themselves began to study systematically the earlier centuries of their city and empire. Yet these historians had little more direct evidence for the earliest phases of Rome’s history than modern historians do. In some respects, they may even have had less, since no documents or archives from the earliest period had survived. Their ‘histories’ of the foundation of ancient Rome tell us a good deal about how the Romans viewed their city and about their values and failings. However, they tell us very little about the subject they claim to describe: what earliest Rome was actually like. One fact is clear. Rome was already a very old city by 63 BCE, when its first emperor was born. But how, then, can we obtain reliable information about the origins of Rome?

One approach is to look beyond the histories of Roman writers for clues in the Latin language or in later Roman institutions that may point back to features of earliest Rome. Archaeological evidence, however, is much more tangible. Dig deep beneath Rome’s visible ancient monuments, and traces of a much earlier settlement—or settlements—survive. Beneath the Forum itself, an ancient marketplace at the centre of the city, lie the remains of an early cemetery, which caused tremendous excitement when first unearthed at the start of the 20th century. Cemeteries imply the existence of a community, and the faint outlines of huts found beneath several parts of the later city may represent traces of such a community. These include remains on the Palatine, the most central of Rome’s seven hills. We know little about the nature of these huts beyond the fact that they were constructed from wood, clay and thatch, and still less about the way of life associated with them. But some of these gaps can be filled by looking just outside Rome. One of the best-preserved and most carefully excavated early structures was found at Fidenae, a few miles north of the city, in the 1980s. The building was rectangular, about six by five metres, and made of wood and rammed earth—a construction method still used today—with a simple porch around it formed by the overhanging roof. Inside were a central hearth, large pottery storage jars, and traces of typical foodstuffs and domestic animals.

There are vivid glimpses here of human life and other forms of life, but the question is what these glimpses add up to. The archaeological remains certainly demonstrate that there is a long and rich prehistory behind the ancient Rome we can still see, but how far back that prehistory extends is another matter.

Part of the problem lies in the conditions under which excavation takes place in the city itself. Rome has been so intensively built on over the centuries that traces of early occupation survive only in areas that have escaped later disturbance. The foundations dug in the first and second centuries CE for the vast marble temples of the Forum obliterated much of what then lay beneath the surface, while the cellars of grand Renaissance houses cut through archaeological remains from still earlier periods in other parts of the city. So we have tiny snapshots, never the big picture. This is archaeology at its most difficult and, although new fragments of evidence continue to emerge, the interpretation—and reinterpretation—of that evidence is almost always contested and often controversial. For example, there is continuing debate over whether the small pieces of wattle and daub found during excavations in the Forum in the mid-20th century indicate that an early hut settlement once existed there, or whether they were accidentally brought in with rubble used a few centuries later to raise the ground level. The Forum site, though suitable for a cemetery, would have been rather damp and marshy for a village.

Precise dating is even more contentious. There is no certain independent date for any of the archaeological material from early Rome or the surrounding area, and the age of almost every major find remains disputed. Over many decades, archaeologists have drawn on evidence such as wheel-made pottery, which is assumed to be later than handmade pottery; Greek ceramics found occasionally in graves, whose dating is better established but still imperfect; and careful comparisons between sites. Together, these indicators have produced only a rough chronological scheme for the period from around 1000 to 600 BCE.

On that basis, the earliest burials in Rome would date to around 1000 BCE, and the earliest known settlements to around 750–700 BCE. Even these dates, however, are far from certain. Alternative scientific dating methods, including radiocarbon analysis, which estimates the age of organic material, have suggested that the conventional dates may underestimate the true age of the remains by as much as a century. The building at Fidenae, for example, was dated to around the middle of the eighth century BCE according to traditional archaeological criteria, whereas radiocarbon analysis places it around the end of the ninth century BCE. If anything, Rome appears to be getting older.
